answer.answer: Gross margin isn't a meaningful metric for JPMorgan Chase, so I did not test whether it moved by more than about 2% a year. As a bank, JPM has no cost of goods sold. Its income statement shows net interest income (interest earned minus interest paid) plus noninterest revenue (fees, markets/trading, investment securities gains or losses), adding up to total net revenue, before credit-loss provisions and noninterest expense. Better measures of how steady its earnings are include net interest margin (net yield on interest-earning assets), the efficiency ratio (noninterest expense ÷ total net revenue), pre-provision profit and return on tangible common equity. For example, net interest income was $12,889M in Q1 2021, $13,872M in Q1 2022 and $20,711M in Q1 2023, so the closest thing to a 'margin' here moves with interest rates.

answer.answer: Verizon's quick ratio at the end of FY2022 was about 0.54x: cash plus net receivables were $27,111M against current liabilities of $50,171M. That is down from 0.57x in FY2021 and well below the usual 1.0x benchmark, so its liquidity does not look healthy on this measure alone. The quick ratio is still a relevant measure (inventory is small, so it differs little from the current ratio of about 0.75x), but large telecoms with steady subscription cash flows and easy access to debt markets often run below 1.0x, so it should be read alongside cash flow and credit access, which I did not check.

answer.answer: Gross margin doesn't work well for American Express. It is a card issuer, payment network and lender, so it reports no cost of goods sold or gross profit. Its top line is 'total revenues net of interest expense' ($52,862M in FY2022, up 25%), and its main costs are provisions for credit losses, Card Member rewards, marketing and salaries. A better measure is pretax margin (pretax income ÷ revenues net of interest expense), which I calculated as falling from 25.2% in FY2021 to 18.1% in FY2022 (18.1% is the key figure below). Revenue grew in every line, driven by billed business up 23% and loans up 22%, but the margin fell mainly because credit provisions swung from a $1,419M release to a $2,182M charge, and total expenses rose 24%, led by rewards, business development and Card Member services.

answer.answer: Operating margin doesn't really fit American Express. It is a bank holding company, so interest is part of how it makes money, and its income statement has no operating income line. The closest measure, pretax income divided by total revenues net of interest expense, fell from 25.2% in 2021 to 18.1% in 2022 (it was 11.9% in 2020). So the reported margin did not improve in 2022, mostly because 2021 benefited from $1,419M of credit-loss reserve releases while 2022 carried $2,182M of provisions; with provisions stripped out, the margin was roughly flat (21.9% in 2021 vs 22.3% in 2022).
answer.calculation: Pretax margin = pretax income / total revenues net of interest expense. FY2022: 9,585/52,862 = 18.13%. FY2021: 10,689/42,380 = 25.22%. FY2020: 4,296/36,087 = 11.90%. Margin before credit-loss provisions = (pretax income + provisions) / revenues net of interest expense. FY2022: (9,585+2,182)/52,862 = 22.26%. FY2021: (10,689−1,419)/42,380 = 21.87%.
